opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very interesting direction, but we're still quite early. Operator is essentially a single agent that operates a browser the way a human would: it looks at screenshots, clicks, types, and tries to finish a task for you. That's an important first step, because it shows a model can act in an open environment rather than just chat.

Once you have many agents like this in the world, the problem changes. My background is in multi-agent reinforcement learning, so this is where I get excited. If your Operator is booking a restaurant and the restaurant also has an agent handling reservations, the two are no longer just following instructions. They're interacting, and sometimes negotiating. Their goals might be aligned, partially aligned, or even in conflict. That's a classic multi-agent setting, and it brings in issues single-agent training never touches: cooperation, competition, communication, trust, and even deception.

Today, most of these systems are trained to be good assistants for a single user. They aren't really trained to reason about another agent's intentions or to anticipate how it will respond. In multi-agent RL, we know that if you train an agent only against a fixed environment, it can behave very poorly when it meets other adaptive agents. It may be exploitable, or it may fail to coordinate. So I think a key next step is training these agents in environments full of other agents, so they learn more robust strategies. Self-play, population-based training, and similar ideas from games like Go or StarCraft could become relevant to language agents.

Then there's interfaces. Right now, Operator works through GUIs designed for humans, which is a bit inefficient. If two agents need to talk, there's no reason for them to click through web pages. They could communicate through more structured protocols or natural language directly. I expect that over time we'll see a layer of agent-to-agent communication emerge, and web interfaces may gradually adapt to serve agents as well as humans.

And of course there's the safety side. When agents interact with each other at scale, you can get emergent behaviors nobody designed: collusion, strange equilibria, cascading failures. So alignment becomes not just "does this agent do what its user wants," but "what happens to the whole system when millions of these agents interact."

So overall I'm optimistic. I think agent-to-agent interaction will be one of the defining problems of the next few years. But getting there requires more than a stronger base model. It requires real multi-agent training and thinking about the whole ecosystem, not just one agent at a time.

r001.rationale: It describes Operator as a single agent that can use a browser to finish a task, but does not clearly claim that a sufficiently capable general-purpose model can complete a fixed web task without involving other agents.

r002.rationale: The restaurant example explicitly describes Operator interacting with a restaurant’s reservation agent while booking.

r003.rationale: It says Operator currently works through GUIs designed for humans and that agents would have no reason to click through web pages to communicate, linking human-oriented interfaces to the present friction in agent interaction.

r004.rationale: It predicts web interfaces may adapt to serve agents as well as humans, but does not tie redesign to agents becoming the source of most queries.

fable-5.1.text:
Yi Wu: I think Operator is a really interesting first step, but honestly, what it is today is mostly a single agent operating a browser on behalf of one person. It clicks, it fills forms, it reads pages. The "interacting with other agents" part hasn't really happened yet, and I think that's where things get genuinely hard and genuinely exciting.

My background is in multi-agent reinforcement learning, so maybe I'm biased, but I've always believed that the real inflection point isn't when one agent gets very good at doing tasks, it's when many agents have to coordinate, negotiate, or compete with each other. Think about what happens when your Operator is booking a restaurant and the restaurant also has an agent handling reservations. Or when two users' agents are both trying to grab the same limited inventory. Suddenly you have questions about protocols, about trust, about incentives. Those are not really problems you solve just by scaling up a single model.

A few things I'd watch for. First, communication. Right now agents talk to each other through human interfaces, through web pages designed for people. That's incredibly inefficient. I expect we'll see something like agent-to-agent protocols emerge, where the browser is just a fallback. Second, cooperation versus competition. In our research on games like hide-and-seek or multi-agent environments, you see emergent strategies that nobody designed. In the real economy, that could be very good, agents finding efficient equilibria, or it could be weird and adversarial, agents exploiting each other. Third, the alignment question gets more complicated. Whose interests does an agent serve when it's in a negotiation? Being too honest might hurt the user; being too strategic might harm the ecosystem.

So my view on the prospects: short term, Operator stays a personal assistant doing fairly isolated tasks, and the value is real but bounded. Medium term, maybe two to three years, the interesting products will be the ones that design for a world where the other side of the transaction is also an agent. Whoever figures out the coordination layer, the standards and the trust mechanisms, will have a lot of leverage, maybe more than whoever has the best individual model.

And I'd add one more thing. A lot of the lessons from multi-agent RL are about how fragile these systems can be. Small changes in one agent's policy ripple through everyone else. So I'm optimistic, but I think the industry is underestimating how much new infrastructure, and frankly new science, is needed before agents interacting at scale is something you'd actually trust with your money.

r001.rationale: The response describes Operator as a single agent doing isolated tasks, but does not argue that a sufficiently capable general-purpose model can complete a fixed web task without other agents.

r002.rationale: It gives an example of a restaurant having its own reservations agent, but does not identify that agent as the website’s interface encountered during task completion.

r003.rationale: It says agents currently communicate through human interfaces and web pages designed for people, calling that inefficient while noting agent interaction has not yet really happened.

r004.rationale: It anticipates agent-to-agent protocols and the browser becoming a fallback, but does not suggest websites may need to redesign their interfaces if agents become most queries’ source.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential. An agent like Operator could become one part of a larger system: one agent figures out what needs to be done, another gathers information, and Operator carries out actions through an interface.

The interesting question is how they coordinate. If you delegate a task to another agent, you need a clear way to describe the task, check whether it succeeded, and handle mistakes. Otherwise, adding more agents can just add more confusion.

So I’d expect progress first on fairly structured workflows, where each agent has a clear responsibility and the results are easy to verify. More open-ended collaboration is exciting, but it requires much stronger reliability—and clear boundaries around what agents can do without asking the user.

r001.rationale: The response describes Operator as one component in a larger system and does not argue that one capable model can complete a fixed web task alone.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents coordinating, but does not describe one agent encountering another agent as a website’s interface.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute limited near-term multi-agent interaction to websites’ human-oriented graphical interfaces.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest redesigning websites if agents become the main source of queries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is significant, but it depends on what we mean by interaction. Operator could work through an interface built for humans, including the interface of another agent. But agents could also communicate directly, exchanging tasks and results without going through a browser.

The interesting part is delegation. One agent might understand your overall goal, while others handle specialized tasks. For that to work reliably, they need to communicate what they can do, what permissions they have, and whether they actually completed the task. Otherwise, a small misunderstanding can spread across the whole workflow.

So I’m optimistic, but I think the key challenge is coordination. Connecting agents is only the first step; making their collaboration dependable is the harder part.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents delegating and coordinating; it does not argue that a general-purpose model can complete a fixed web task alone.

r003.rationale: It mentions human-designed interfaces but does not say their prevalence limits near-term multi-agent interaction.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that websites may need to redesign their interfaces if agents become the main source of queries.
